mayor noun

also lord mayor, mayoress, village mayor

modern

Traupman 22, 179, 344
M-O s.v. city council: mayor

praefectus urbī

noun phrase: praefectus, praefectī m., with the dative urbī

Traupman’s word for a modern mayor, and Morgan–Owens’s first (as urbis praefectus, after Vives). Classically the prefect of the city of Rome: under the Republic the consuls’ deputy while they were away, under the emperors a standing office with its own jurisdiction (Lewis & Short, s.v. praeficiō). A Roman town had no single mayor, but two magistrates elected for a year, the duovirī.

Other words

  • duovirī, duovirōrum m. pl. — the two chief magistrates of a Roman town

    noun, second declension, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Agr. 2.93 (Lewis & Short)

    The highest magistrates of the mūnicipia and colonies (Lewis & Short, who head the word duovir and call duumvir less correct). The nearest Roman thing to a mayor; at Capua they wanted to be called praetors instead (Cic. Agr. 2.93).

  • magister vīcī — the head of a ward or a village

    noun phrase: magister, magistrī m., with the genitive vīcī · also used · classical · Suet. Aug. 30: hōs magistrī ē plēbe cujusque vīcīniae lēctī; M-O s.v. city council: mayor

    At Rome the overseers of the city’s wards (vīcī), chosen from the people of each neighbourhood (Suet. Aug. 30; Lewis & Short, s.v. magister). A vīcus is also a village, so the title suits a village mayor; Morgan–Owens lists it among the words for a mayor.

  • major, majōris m. — mayor (the medieval title)

    noun, third declension · also used · medieval · Traupman 179

    The title from which English mayor and French maire come; Traupman lists it. In classical Latin it is only the comparative, greater or elder.

Examples

  • Immō proavus tuus ōlim erat praefectus urbī.

    Well, your great-grandfather was once mayor of the city.Traupman 22

See also town hall, council, town, city, village, office.
